title: Surface Energy and Surface Tension
short_intro: Surface energy is the extra potential energy possessed by molecules at the surface of a liquid due to unbalanced intermolecular attractive forces. Surface tension is numerically equal to the work done in increasing the surface area by unity under isothermal conditions.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of surface tension, molecular theory of surface tension, relation between surface energy and surface tension, excess pressure inside liquid drops and soap bubbles, angle of contact, and capillary rise.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Work done in blowing bubbles, splitting and coalescence of liquid drops, thermodynamics of surface films, temperature dependence of surface tension, and rigorous derivation of capillary height accounting for meniscus.

prerequisites: Intermolecular forces and range of molecular attraction
Work, energy, and conservation principles in mechanics
Hydrostatics and pressure distribution in fluids

concept_notes.heading: Molecular Theory of Surface Tension
bullets: Molecules deep inside a liquid experience equal attractive forces from surrounding molecules in all directions, resulting in a net zero force.
Molecules located within a surface layer of thickness equal to the molecular range (sphere of influence) experience a net downward attractive force due to the absence of upper liquid molecules.
To bring a molecule from the interior of the liquid to the surface, work must be done against this inward resultant force, which gets stored as potential energy at the surface.

concept_notes.heading: Surface Energy vs Surface Tension
bullets: Surface tension (T or σ) is defined as the force acting per unit length imaginarilly drawn on the liquid surface, perpendicular to the line, with dimensions [ML&sup0;T&sup-2;].
Surface energy (E) is the potential energy per unit surface area of the liquid film, with dimensions [MT&sup-2;].
Numerically and dimensionally, surface tension and surface energy per unit area are identical, expressed in J m&sup-2; or N m&sup-1;.

concept_notes.heading: Excess Pressure across Curved Surfaces
bullets: Due to surface tension, molecules on a curved liquid surface pull inward, creating a pressure difference between the concave and convex sides.
For a spherical liquid drop of radius R, the excess pressure is given by P = 2T / R.
For a soap bubble in air, which has two free surfaces (inner and outer), the excess pressure is given by P = 4T / R.

concept_notes.heading: Capillarity and Angle of Contact
bullets: The angle of contact (θ) is the angle subtended by the tangent to the liquid surface at the point of contact with the solid surface, measured inside the liquid.
Liquids that wet glass (e.g., water) form a concave meniscus and have an acute angle of contact (θ < 90°), showing capillary rise.
Liquids that do not wet glass (e.g., mercury) form a convex meniscus and have an obtuse angle of contact (θ > 90°), showing capillary depression.

derivations.title: Work Done in Increasing Surface Area and Surface Energy Relation
derivations.conditions: Isothermal expansion of a rectangular liquid film on a wire frame with one movable wire of length l.
steps: Let a wire frame support a liquid film of length l. The film has two free surfaces (front and back), so the total effective length of the surface acting against the pulling force is 2l.
If the movable wire is pulled outward by a small distance dx, the increase in total surface area of the film is dA = 2 * l * dx.
The magnitude of the inward pulling force due to surface tension is F = T * (2l).
The work done (dW) in pulling the wire by distance dx is dW = F * dx = (T * 2l) * dx = T * (2 * l * dx) = T * dA.
This work done is stored in the film as potential surface energy (dU). Thus, dU = T * dA, which implies T = dU / dA.
derivations.result: Surface tension is equal to the surface energy per unit surface area (T = E).

derivations.title: Jurin's Law: Rise of Liquid in a Capillary Tube
derivations.conditions: A capillary tube of radius r dipped in a liquid of surface tension T and density ρ with contact angle θ.
steps: Let the liquid rise to a height h in the capillary tube. The upper meniscus is hemispherical of radius r, such that r = R cos(θ), where R is the radius of curvature of the meniscus.
The upward force supporting the liquid column is due to the vertical component of surface tension acting along the circumference of the meniscus: F_up = (2 π r) * T * cos(θ).
The downward force is the weight of the liquid column of height h (including the meniscus correction): F_down = m * g = (π r^2 * h) * ρ * g.
Equating the upward and downward forces for equilibrium: (2 π r) * T * cos(θ) = π r^2 * h * ρ * g.
Solving for capillary rise h gives h = (2 T cos(θ)) / (r ρ g).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Variation of Surface Tension with Temperature
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A linear downward sloping graph of Surface Tension (T) on the y-axis versus Temperature (T_c in Celsius) on the x-axis, meeting zero at the critical temperature.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Surface tension decreases linearly with an increase in temperature because thermal agitation increases average molecular separation, reducing cohesive forces.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct conceptual questions and numerical calculations involving temperature coefficients.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius 2 cm. Given the surface tension of soap solution is 0.03 N m⁻¹.
solution_steps: Identify given values: Radius R = 2 cm = 0.02 m, Surface tension T = 0.03 N m&sup-1;.
Recall that a soap bubble has two free surfaces, so the excess pressure formula is P = 4T / R.
Calculate the final value: P = 0.12 / 0.02 = 6 Pa.

solved_numericals.question: 8 identical water drops, each of radius r = 1 mm, merge to form a single large drop. If the surface tension of water is 0.072 N m⁻¹, calculate the amount of energy liberated in this process.
solution_steps: Equating volumes of 8 small drops to one large drop: (4/3) * π * R^3 = 8 * ((4/3) * π * r^3).
Simplify to find the radius of the big drop: R^3 = 8r^3 => R = 2r = 2 * 1 mm = 2 mm = 2 * 10&sup-3; m.
Initial surface area of 8 drops: A_i = 8 * (4 π r^2) = 32 π r^2.
Final surface area of the big drop: A_f = 4 π R^2 = 4 π (2r)^2 = 16 π r^2.
Decrease in surface area: ΔA = A_i - A_f = 32 π r^2 - 16 π r^2 = 16 π r^2.
Energy liberated (Work done): W = T * ΔA = T * 16 π r^2 = 0.072 * 16 * π * (10&sup-3;)^2.
Compute final numerical value: W = 0.072 * 16 * 3.1416 * 10&sup-6; ≈ 3.62 * 10&sup-6; J.

solved_numericals.question: A capillary tube of internal radius 0.5 mm is dipped vertically into water. To what height does the water rise in the tube? (Surface tension of water = 0.072 N m⁻¹, angle of contact = 0°, density of water = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
solution_steps: List given parameters: r = 0.5 mm = 5 * 10&sup-4; m, T = 0.072 N m&sup-1;, θ = 0° (cosθ = 1), ρ = 1000 kg m&sup-3;, g = 9.8 m s&sup-2;.
Write Jurin's formula for capillary rise: h = (2 T cos(θ)) / (r ρ g).

assumptions_and_limitations: The liquid temperature is assumed constant during isothermal surface area changes; localized heating occurs during rapid adiabatic drops.
Capillary rise formulas assume a perfectly cylindrical tube and a spherical meniscus, which breaks down for large radius tubes where the meniscus flattens.
Surface tension is assumed uniform, ignoring contamination or surfactant impurities that locally alter surface tension.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Surface tension is a force acting downwards into the liquid.
common_misconceptions.correct: Surface tension is a tensile force acting tangentially along the surface of the liquid.
common_misconceptions.why: Forces due to surface tension act along the plane of the liquid surface perpendicular to any imaginary line drawn on it.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A soap bubble has only one surface area to consider for energy calculations.
common_misconceptions.correct: A soap bubble has two free surfaces (inner and outer).
common_misconceptions.why: A very thin liquid film in air exposes both sides to air, doubling the active surface area compared to a solid liquid drop.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Water rises in a capillary tube because of atmospheric pressure pushing it up.
common_misconceptions.correct: Water rises due to the upward component of adhesive forces and surface tension pulling the contact line upward.
common_misconceptions.why: Atmospheric pressure acts equally on all liquid surfaces and does not drive the net upward capillary ascent against gravity.

quick_revision: Surface tension T = F/l = W/ΔA with units N m⁻¹ or J m⁻².
Excess pressure is 2T/R for drops and 4T/R for soap bubbles.
Capillary rise is inversely proportional to tube radius (h ∝ 1/r).
Surface tension decreases linearly with an increase in temperature.
Acute contact angle (θ < 90°) causes wetting and capillary rise; obtuse angle causes depression.
